los.text: Demonstrate the surface anatomy landmarks associated with major thoracic structures
los.html:
LandmarkLevel / marks
Jugular notchT2/3; trachea palpable above it
Sternal angleT4/5, 2nd costal cartilage: carina, aortic arch, azygos joins SVC; count ribs from here
Xiphisternal jointT9; lower border of the heart, central tendon of diaphragm
Nipple (male)4th intercostal space, midclavicular line
Apex beat5th intercostal space, midclavicular line
Diaphragm domes (expiration)Right 5th rib, left 5th intercostal space
ScapulaSpine at T3; inferior angle at T7 (7th rib)
Vertebra prominensC7 spinous process
Lungs and pleura
  • Lung edge at ribs 6 / 8 / 10 (midclavicular, midaxillary, paravertebral)
  • Pleura two ribs lower, 8 / 10 / 12.
Heart outline
  • Upper border 2nd left to 3rd right costal cartilage
  • Right border 3rd–6th right cartilage beside the sternum
  • Inferior border 6th right cartilage to the apex.

los.text: Describe the movements involved in normal, vigorous and forced ventilation and list the muscles responsible for these movements
los.html:
BreathingMusclesHow
Quiet inspirationDiaphragm (main), external intercostalsDiaphragm descends (↑ vertical size); ribs rise: pump-handle (upper ribs, ↑ front-to-back) and bucket-handle (lower ribs, ↑ side-to-side)
Quiet expirationNone (passive)Elastic recoil of lungs and chest wall
Forced inspiration+ Sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, pectoralis major/minor and serratus anterior (with arms fixed)Lift sternum and upper ribs further
Forced expirationAbdominal muscles (rectus, obliques, transversus), internal intercostals, latissimus dorsi (cough)Raise abdominal pressure to push the diaphragm up; pull ribs down
  • Signs of respiratory distress: accessory muscle use, tripod position (fixing the arms lets pectorals lift the ribs).

los.text: Describe the functional anatomy of the intercostal muscles
los.html:
LayerFibres runAction
External intercostalsDown and forward ("hands in pockets"); external intercostal membrane in frontRaise ribs: inspiration
Internal intercostalsDown and back (at right angles to the externals); internal intercostal membrane behindInterosseous part lowers ribs (forced expiration); parasternal part helps inspiration
Innermost intercostals (+ subcostales, transversus thoracis)Same as the internalsDeep to the neurovascular bundle
AlsoKeep the intercostal spaces rigid so they don't suck in or bulge out with pressure swings.
NerveThe intercostal nerve of each space.

los.text: Explain that the arterial supply of the thoracic wall is via intercostal vessels (as branches of the internal thoracic artery and aorta)
los.html:
Posterior intercostal arteries
  • Spaces 1–2 from the superior intercostal artery (costocervical trunk of the subclavian)
  • Spaces 3–11 from the thoracic aorta
  • Subcostal artery below rib 12.
Anterior intercostal arteriesFrom the internal thoracic artery (spaces 1–6) and its musculophrenic branch (7–9).
AnastomosisAnterior and posterior arteries join in each space.
Internal thoracic artery
  • From the subclavian, ~1 cm lateral to the sternum behind the costal cartilages
  • Ends at the 6th space as the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries
  • Used in CABG (LIMA graft).
VeinsPosterior intercostals → azygos/hemiazygos; anterior → internal thoracic veins.
Coarctation of the aorta enlarges the intercostal collaterals, which notch the undersides of the ribs on CXR.

los.text: Describe a neurovascular bundle in a typical intercostal space and outline the structures its components supply
los.html:
Positionin the costal groove on the inferior border of the rib above, between the internal and innermost intercostals.
Order from topVein, Artery, Nerve (VAN).
Intercostal nerve supplies
  • Intercostal muscles
  • Skin of the dermatome (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches)
  • Costal parietal pleura.
  • T7–T11 carry on into the abdominal wall muscles, skin and parietal peritoneum.
Artery suppliesIntercostal muscles, overlying skin, pleura, and the breast (perforators of spaces 2–4).
ClinicalNeedles and drains go just above the upper border of the rib below to miss the main bundle.

los.text: Explain that the intercostal nerves are branches of the ventral primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves and receive rami communicantes from the sympathetic trunk
los.html:
OriginVentral primary rami of T1–T11 (T12 = subcostal nerve); dorsal rami supply the back muscles and skin.
Special
  • Most of T1 joins the brachial plexus
  • T2 gives the intercostobrachial nerve (axilla and medial arm: route for referred cardiac pain).
Sympathetic links
  • Every intercostal nerve receives a grey ramus (postganglionic fibres to sweat glands, vessels, hair muscles)
  • T1–L2 also send white rami (preganglionic) to the sympathetic trunk.
BranchesCollateral, lateral cutaneous (midaxillary), anterior cutaneous, muscular.
ClinicalShingles follows one dermatome; intercostal nerve blocks for rib fractures.

los.text: Recognise normal structures on radiographs of the thorax in inspiration and expiration, and be able to recognise common abnormalities
los.html:
FilmLook
Good inspiration~6 anterior (10 posterior) ribs above the diaphragm; narrow heart
ExpirationDiaphragm high, fewer ribs, heart looks bigger, crowded bases; can make a small pneumothorax easier to see
  • Normal structures: trachea and carina, aortic knuckle, heart borders, hila, costophrenic angles, gastric bubble, ribs, clavicles, scapulae, breast shadows.
AbnormalityAppearance
PneumothoraxVisible pleural edge with no lung markings beyond it
Pleural effusionBlunted costophrenic angle, meniscus
ConsolidationPatchy opacity, air bronchograms, lost border (silhouette sign)
CollapseVolume loss; trachea/mediastinum pulled towards it
Hyperinflation (COPD)>7 anterior ribs, flat diaphragm
Tension pneumothoraxMediastinum pushed away: a clinical diagnosis, treat before X-ray

los.text: Explain the concept of the pleural sac (parietal and visceral) and potential space
los.html:
Pleuraa serous membrane folded into two layers: visceral (stuck to the lung, into the fissures) and parietal (costal, diaphragmatic, mediastinal and cervical parts), continuous around the lung root and pulmonary ligament.
Pleural cavity
  • a potential space with ~5–10 mL of fluid
  • Surface tension couples the lung to the chest wall
  • Pressure is negative (about −5 cmH₂O) so the lung stays expanded.
Picture ita fist pushed into a partly filled balloon.
What fills it in diseaseAir (pneumothorax), fluid (effusion), blood (haemothorax), pus (empyema), lymph (chylothorax).
RecessesCostodiaphragmatic and costomediastinal: spare pleura for the lungs to expand into.

los.text: Identify the surface landmarks that are used when inserting a chest drain
los.html:
Safe triangle
  • Front = lateral border of pectoralis major
  • Back = lateral border of latissimus dorsi
  • Bottom = horizontal line at the 5th intercostal space (nipple level in men)
  • Apex below the axilla.
Site4th–5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line, just above the rib below.
Avoids
  • The intercostal bundle (under the rib above)
  • Internal thoracic artery (in front)
  • Long thoracic nerve (further back on serratus anterior)
  • Liver and spleen (too low).
Needle decompression of tension4th–5th space mid-axillary (adults, current ATLS) or 2nd space midclavicular.
